newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan base metals market report - January 29.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan base metals market report - January 29.

text.p: Prices for Taiwan copper products trended upward during January, reflecting higher import costs during the period, local traders said on Wednesday.
"The recent rise in copper products is a reflection of higher world prices," a buyer at Taiwan's Pacific Electric Wire & Cable Corp said.
Traders noted unconfirmed market talk that South Korea's LG Metals Corp was covering a short position in copper futures, which in turn was supporting short-term futures prices.
"Taiwan metals traders are saying that LG Group's covering has caused the futures market to go upward," a buyer at Taiwan Tai-I International Cable and Wire said.
LG Metals is a unit of South Korea's LG Group LUGG.CN.
Traders said local demand for metals remained sluggish, but that buyers were increasing their aluminium ingot inventories as sharp recent price rises were expected to continue.
Traders said recent aluminium ingot prices had risen to between US$85 to US$90 per tonne on the London Metals Exchange, compared with US$65 per tonne in December.

Traders remained sceptical about the Taiwan government's repeated assertions that a slow economic recovery would fuel a long-awaited rebound in the construction sector, where a deep recession is now in its seventh year.
The value of loans extended by Taiwan banks to construction firms fell 14.96 percent in December 1996 from a year earlier, marked the 20th consecutive month of declines.
"We still haven't seen any signs of economic recovery -- at least not in our (construction metals) sector," the Pacific Wire buyer said.
Central bank officials had attributed the flat-to-negative growth in construction loans to persistent overall sluggishness in the economy.
Under latest government projections, Taiwan's gross domestic product will have grown just 5.7 percent in 1996 -- a full percentage point below the official 6.7 percent target.
Official GDP figures will be reported in late February.
Banks have been particularly cautious in granting loans to firms in the construction sector, which has seen deep recession since the local real estate market peaked in 1989.
Despite its problems, construction remains Taiwan's top sector for basic metals consumption.
